questions.question:
Consider the following two statements.

S1: If a candidate is known to be corrupt, then he will not be elected
S2: If a candidate is kind, he will be elected

Which one of the following statements follows from S1 and S2 as per sound inference rules of logic?

options.A: If a person is known to be corrupt, he is kind
options.B: If a person is not known to be corrupt, he is not kind
options.C: If a person is kind, he is not known to be corrupt
options.D: If a person is not kind, he is not known to be corrupt

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- S1: corrupt [latex]\rightarrow\neg[/latex] elected, whose contrapositive is elected [latex]\rightarrow\neg[/latex] corrupt
- S2: kind [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] elected

Chaining: kind [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] elected [latex]\rightarrow\neg[/latex] corrupt.

Answer: If a person is kind, he is not known to be corrupt

questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for a group [latex]G[/latex]?

options.A: If for all [latex]x,y \in G, (xy)^2=x^2y^2[/latex], then [latex]G[/latex] is commutative.
options.B: If for all [latex]x \in G, x^2=1[/latex], then [latex]G[/latex] is commutative. Here, 1 is the identity element of [latex]G[/latex].
options.C: If the order of [latex]G[/latex] is 2 , then [latex]G[/latex] is commutative.
options.D: If [latex]G[/latex] is commutative, then a subgroup of [latex]G[/latex] need not be commutative.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- [latex](xy)^2=x^2y^2[/latex] means [latex]xyxy=xxyy[/latex]. Cancel x on the left and y on the right: [latex]yx=xy[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]x^2=1[/latex] means every element is its own inverse. Then [latex]xy=(xy)^{-1}=y^{-1}x^{-1}=yx[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- A group of order 2 is [latex]\{1,a\}[/latex], which is cyclic, hence commutative [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Every subgroup of a commutative group is commutative (same operation) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

Let p,q, r, s represent the following propositions.

p: x[latex]\in[/latex]{8,9,10,11,12}
q: x is a composite number
r: x is a perfect square
s: x is a prime number

The integer x[latex]\geq[/latex]2 which satisfies [latex]\neg((p\Rightarrow q)\wedge (\neg r \vee \neg s))[/latex] is ________.
questions.explanation:
[latex] eg((p\Rightarrow q)\wedge( eg r\vee eg s))\equiv(p\wedge eg q)\vee(r\wedge s)[/latex]

- [latex]r\wedge s[/latex] (perfect square and prime) is impossible.
- So we need [latex]p\wedge eg q[/latex]: x in {8, 9, 10, 11, 12} and not composite. Only 11 qualifies.

Answer: 11

questions.question:
Let [latex] P [/latex] be the partial order defined on the set [latex] \{1,2,3,4\} [/latex] as follows
[latex] P=\{(x, x) \mid x \in\{1,2,3,4\}\} \cup\{(1,2),(3,2),(3,4)\} [/latex]
The number of total orders on [latex] \{1,2,3,4\} [/latex] that contain [latex] P [/latex] is ______
questions.explanation:
A total order containing P must keep [latex]1 \lt 2,\ 3 \lt 2,\ 3 \lt 4[/latex]. Count such orderings (linear extensions).

The first element must be 1 or 3 (nothing must come before them).
- Start with 1: next must be 3 (both 2 and 4 need 3 first), then 2, 4 in any order [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1324, 1342 (2 orders).
- Start with 3: arrange 1, 2, 4 with 1 before 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3124, 3142, 3412 (3 orders).

Total = 5

Answer: 5

questions.question: Let [latex]f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} [/latex] be a function such that [latex]f(x)=\max \left\{x, x^3\right\}, x \in \mathbb{R} [/latex], where [latex]\mathbb{R} [/latex] is the set of all real numbers. The set of all points where [latex]f(x) [/latex] is NOT differentiable is
questions.explanation:
Compare [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]x^3[/latex]: they are equal at [latex]x=-1,0,1[/latex]. So [latex]f(x)=x[/latex] for [latex]x\le -1[/latex], [latex]x^3[/latex] on [latex][-1,0][/latex], [latex]x[/latex] on [latex][0,1][/latex], [latex]x^3[/latex] for [latex]x\ge1[/latex].

At every switching point the two pieces have different slopes ([latex]\frac{d}{dx}x=1[/latex], [latex]\frac{d}{dx}x^3=3x^2[/latex]):
- [latex]x=-1[/latex]: slopes [latex]1[/latex] and [latex]3[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner
- [latex]x=0[/latex]: slopes [latex]0[/latex] and [latex]1[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner
- [latex]x=1[/latex]: slopes [latex]1[/latex] and [latex]3[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner

Everywhere else [latex]f[/latex] is a polynomial, hence differentiable.

Answer: [latex]\{-1,0,1\}[/latex]

questions.question:
For two different persons [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex], the predicate [latex]M(x, y)[/latex] denotes that [latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex].
Consider the following statement.

There is a person who does not know anyone else, but that person is known by everyone else.

Which one of the following expressions represents the above statement?

options.A: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
options.B: [latex](\forall y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
options.C: [latex](\exists y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
options.D: [latex](\forall y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]

questions.explanation:
We need to translate: "There is a person [latex]y[/latex] such that [latex]y[/latex] doesn't know anyone else, but everyone else knows [latex]y[/latex]."

- "There is a person [latex]y[/latex]" → [latex](\exists y)[/latex].
- "for every other person [latex]x[/latex] ([latex]x\ne y[/latex])" → [latex](\forall x)(x\ne y\rightarrow\ldots)[/latex].
- "[latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex]" (everyone else knows this person) → [latex]M(x,y)[/latex].
- "[latex]y[/latex] does not know [latex]x[/latex]" (this person doesn't know anyone else) → [latex]\neg M(y,x)[/latex].

Combining: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)\big((x\ne y)\rightarrow(M(x,y)\wedge\neg M(y,x))\big)[/latex] — there exists such a special person [latex]y[/latex], and for every other person [latex]x[/latex], [latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex] but [latex]y[/latex] does not know [latex]x[/latex].

The other options either use [latex]\forall y[/latex] (wrongly requiring every person to have this property, instead of just one special person), or use [latex]\exists x[/latex] (existentially quantifying [latex]x[/latex] instead of requiring it for every other person), which don't match the intended meaning.

Answer: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)\left((x\neq y)\rightarrow(M(x,y)\wedge\neg M(y,x))\right)[/latex]

questions.question: Let [latex]G[/latex] be an undirected graph, which is a path on [latex]8[/latex] vertices. The number of matchings in [latex]G[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
Let [latex]f(k)[/latex] denote the number of matchings (including the empty matching) in a path graph with [latex]k[/latex] edges. Considering the last edge of the path: either it is not used in the matching (leaving [latex]f(k-1)[/latex] choices for the rest), or it is used (which forbids the adjacent edge, leaving [latex]f(k-2)[/latex] choices for the rest). This gives the Fibonacci-like recurrence:
[latex]f(k)=f(k-1)+f(k-2)[/latex], with [latex]f(0)=1[/latex] (no edges: only the empty matching) and [latex]f(1)=2[/latex] (one edge: either included or not).

[latex]f(2)=3,\ f(3)=5,\ f(4)=8,\ f(5)=13,\ f(6)=21,\ f(7)=34[/latex].

A path on [latex]8[/latex] vertices has [latex]7[/latex] edges, so the number of matchings is [latex]f(7)=34[/latex].

Answer: 34

questions.question:
Consider a probability distribution given by the density function [latex] P(x) [/latex].

[latex] P(x) = \begin{cases} Cx^2, &\text{for } 1 \leq x \leq 4 \\ 0, & \text{for }x < 1 \text{ or } x > 4 \end{cases}[/latex]

The probability that [latex] x [/latex] lies between 2 and 3, i.e., [latex] P(2 \leq x \leq 3) [/latex] is _________. (rounded off to three decimal places)
questions.explanation:
First find [latex]C[/latex] using the normalization condition [latex]\int_1^4Cx^2\,dx=1[/latex]:
[latex]C\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4=C\cdot\dfrac{64-1}{3}=21C=1\ \Rightarrow\ C=\dfrac1{21}[/latex]

[latex]P(2\le x\le3)=\displaystyle\int_2^3\dfrac{x^2}{21}\,dx=\dfrac1{21}\left[\dfrac{x^3}3\right]_2^3=\dfrac1{21}\cdot\dfrac{27-8}3=\dfrac1{21}\cdot\dfrac{19}3=\dfrac{19}{63}\approx0.302[/latex]

Answer: 0.302

questions.question:
Let [latex]\mathcal{F} [/latex] be the set of all functions from [latex]\{1, \dots, n\} [/latex] to [latex]\{0,1\} [/latex]. Define the binary relation [latex]\preceq [/latex] on [latex]\mathcal{F} [/latex] as follows:
[latex] \forall f, g \in \mathcal{F}, \, f \preceq g \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \forall x \in \{1, \dots, n\}, f(x) \leq g(x), \text{ where } 0 \leq 1. [/latex]
Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
questions.explanation:
[latex]f\preceq g[/latex] iff [latex]f(x)\le g(x)[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex] — this is the standard pointwise "less than or equal to" ordering on binary functions.

- Reflexive: [latex]f(x)\le f(x)[/latex] always. Antisymmetric: if [latex]f\preceq g[/latex] and [latex]g\preceq f[/latex], then [latex]f(x)=g(x)[/latex] for all [latex]x[/latex], so [latex]f=g[/latex]. Transitive: chains through in the obvious way. So [latex]\preceq[/latex] is a genuine partial order (not symmetric, and not an equivalence relation, since e.g. [latex]f\preceq g[/latex] doesn't imply [latex]g\preceq f[/latex] unless [latex]f=g[/latex]).

- Lattice: for any two functions [latex]f,g[/latex], their pointwise max (taking [latex]\max(f(x),g(x))[/latex] at every [latex]x[/latex]) is their least upper bound, and their pointwise min is their greatest lower bound — both always exist within [latex]\mathcal F[/latex]. So [latex](\mathcal F,\preceq)[/latex] is indeed a lattice.

Answer: (F,⪯) is a partial order; and (F,⪯) is a lattice.

questions.question:
Consider the two statements.

S1: There exist random variables [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] such that [latex]\left(\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E(X))(Y-\mathbb E(Y))]\right)^2 > \textsf{Var}[X]\textsf{Var}[Y][/latex]
S2: For all random variables [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex], [latex]\textsf{Cov}[X,Y]=\mathbb E \left[|X-\mathbb E[X]||Y-\mathbb E[Y]|\right ][/latex]

Which one of the following choices is correct?

options.A: Both S1 and S2 are true.
options.B: S1 is true, but S2 is false.
options.C: S1 is false, but S2 is true.
options.D: Both S1 and S2 are false.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- S1: the left side is [latex]Cov(X,Y)^2[/latex]. By Cauchy-Schwarz, [latex]Cov(X,Y)^2\le Var(X)Var(Y)[/latex] always, so S1 is FALSE.
- S2: the right side is always [latex]\ge0[/latex], but covariance can be negative (e.g. Y = [latex]-[/latex]X) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Both S1 and S2 are false

questions.question:
Let [latex]X[/latex] be a set and [latex]2^X[/latex] denote the powerset of [latex]X[/latex].
Define a binary operation [latex] \Delta [/latex] on [latex]2^X[/latex] as follows:
[latex]A \Delta B=(A-B) \cup (B-A)[/latex]
Let [latex] H=(2^X,\Delta ) [/latex]. Which of the following statements about [latex]H[/latex] is/are correct?

options.B: Every element in [latex]H[/latex] has an inverse, but [latex]H[/latex] is NOT a group.
options.C: For every [latex]A \in 2^X[/latex], the inverse of [latex]A[/latex] is the complement of [latex]A[/latex].
options.D: For every [latex]A \in 2^X[/latex], the inverse of [latex]A[/latex] is [latex]A[/latex].

questions.explanation:
Check the group properties of symmetric difference on [latex]2^X[/latex]:
- Closed: [latex]A\Delta B\subseteq X[/latex]
- Associative: yes (it behaves like XOR on membership)
- Identity: [latex]\phi[/latex], since [latex]A\Delta\phi=A[/latex]
- Inverse: [latex]A\Delta A=\phi[/latex], so every A is its own inverse (not its complement: [latex]A\Delta A^c=X[/latex])

Answer: H is a group; the inverse of A is A
